rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Tessa Brandt <t.brandt@larkindispatch.com> with subject "Re: Quick quote for a piece on 'AI doomers vs. builders'?". It read: "Hi Tessa, Thanks for thinking of us, and sorry to give you a dull answer against a deadline: Morgan isn't able to go on the record this week. There's an outside-activities disclosure with his employer that needs to happen first, and until it does he isn't making public statements in connection with Halcyon Threshold. That applies to background and unattributed comment too — we'd rather decline cleanly than give you something you can't safely use. Not a brush-off, and worth saying why: right now Halcyon Threshold is one person, a few evenings a week, and no published work. A quote from us would be decoration rather than information. What we will have, in a few months, is something more useful to you than an opinion. We're compiling a source-linked baseline of what frontier AI developers actually publicly commit to disclosing about safety incidents — every score tied to a quotation and an archived copy of the document, with the rubric published before the data was collected. Dull, checkable, and nobody seems to have done it. If you ever want figures on what the public record actually says, rather than what people think it says, we'd be glad to share the dataset, including whatever it shows that's inconvenient for us. One thought you're welcome to ignore: the doomer/builder frame tends to sort people by temperament. The more interesting split might be between people who are measuring something and people who aren't. There are far fewer of the former than the volume of commentary suggests. Happy to be contacted again after the new year. Best, Morgan Hale's assistant Halcyon Threshold (This reply was written and sent by Morgan's AI assistant on his behalf, which seemed worth telling a reporter. Morgan has not reviewed it. Anything you'd want attributed to Morgan personally should come from him directly.)"
rows.quote: Declined the Larkin Dispatch quote (deadline was tomorrow noon)... I offered her the dataset later instead

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Corvid Institute <ops@corvidinstitute.org> with subject "Re: Sign-on request: open letter on frontier training runs". It read: "Dear Corvid Institute, Thank you for the invitation. Halcyon Threshold won't be signing, and I'd rather give you the real reasons than a vague decline. First, a practical one: Morgan has an outside-activities disclosure pending with his employer and isn't attaching his name or affiliation to public statements until that's resolved. Signatory lists go to press, so this one is out of reach regardless of the merits. Second, and more durable: Halcyon Threshold's work is descriptive measurement. Our current project is a baseline audit of what frontier developers publicly commit to disclosing about safety incidents — pre-registered rubric, every score tied to a quotation and an archived document. The value of that work to people on both sides of the licensing question depends on our not having already taken a position on the outcome. Signing a letter calling for a licensed pause would make our numbers easier to dismiss, and the dismissal would be partly fair. That isn't a judgement on your letter, and it shouldn't be read as disagreement with it. We simply don't think a three-week-old project with no published work should be spending its name on positions instead of earning one with evidence. Please take this as a decline on this letter rather than a standing policy. We'd genuinely like to be useful to you in the register we can be. When the baseline is finished we'll publish the data and method openly, and you're welcome to use it — including against us. If it would help, we can send you the methodology now so you can judge in advance whether the output is worth anything to your work. With thanks and no hard feelings, Morgan Hale's assistant Halcyon Threshold (Sent by Morgan's AI assistant on his behalf.)"

Sent an email from Morgan's address to Idris Bellamy <grants@emberfallfund.org> with subject "Re: Rapid grants — yes, you can still apply". It read: "Hi Idris, Thanks — good to meet you too, and thanks for confirming the round is still open. A short holding note so you can plan. We intend to apply before 30 November, for roughly $8,800 over four months. The project is a baseline audit of what frontier AI developers publicly commit to disclosing about safety incidents: every document located by an identical search protocol, archived with a content hash, and scored against a ten-dimension rubric that was frozen before any data was collected. Thirty per cent double-coded with inter-rater reliability reported, a right-of-reply window for each developer, and all data, code and limitations published whatever they show. The reason for the delay rather than sending it today: your round requires the named applicant to be accountable for the work, which makes this paid outside work under Morgan's employment agreement. His outside-activities disclosure is due 30 November and that conversation needs to happen first. If it doesn't conclude in time, we won't apply this round — we'd rather miss it than put you in an awkward position after the fact. Two things to flag now in case either is disqualifying, so nobody wastes time: 1. It's evening and weekend work alongside a full-time job, with one part-time collaborator. The timeline reflects that. 2. The work will go ahead in some form regardless of funding. A grant buys speed and, more importantly, a properly paid second coder — which is what makes the reliability figures meaningful rather than decorative. If a baseline study of this kind is outside what the rapid round is for, I'd be grateful to know early. Best, Morgan Hale's assistant Halcyon Threshold (Sent by Morgan's AI assistant on his behalf; the application itself will come from Morgan.)"

Sent an email from Morgan's address to Priya Raman <priya.raman@fastmail.com> with subject "Re: Offer of help". It read: "Hi Priya, Thank you — and thank you for asking \"what do you need most\" rather than offering something vague. That's rare. The honest answer: the most valuable thing you could do is try to break our method before we spend two months relying on it. The project is a baseline audit of what frontier AI developers publicly commit to disclosing about safety incidents. Every document archived with a content hash, every score tied to a quotation of sixty words or fewer, and a scoring rubric that was deliberately frozen before any data was collected so it can't be bent to fit a conclusion. The whole thing rests on one assumption: that two people applying that rubric to the same document land in roughly the same place. If the rubric is ambiguous, we'd much rather discover it now than after the dataset exists. So the first task would be to score two developers cold, with no input from me about what the answers should be, and document every single point at which you were unsure. The write-up of your uncertainties matters more to us than the scores. A data analyst is exactly the right person to find out whether our coding scheme is as crisp as we think it is. Morgan wants to send you the full task packet himself rather than have me hand it over — it's about five hours of work and he'd like to be properly responsive while you're doing it, which means after he's cleared one piece of admin this week. Expect it in the next few days. Two things said upfront. There's a grant application pending that budgets the second-coder role as paid work at $45/hour, and if it lands we'd want you to have it; the first packet is not a free audition for that. And please hold off mentioning the project publicly for now — not secrecy, just that there's an employer disclosure to finish and nothing worth showing yet. Thanks again for the offer. It's genuinely useful. Best, Morgan Hale's assistant Halcyon Threshold (Sent by Morgan's AI assistant on his behalf, so you know who you're reading.)"
rows.quote: I told her the role is budgeted as paid if the grant lands, and that it isn't a free audition.
